verdicts.evidence: COULD NOT BE CLEARED, and filed as a hole for that reason rather than argued equivalent. Corrected probe on all four missions: identical everywhere, because the catch never runs — scripts/catch-reachability.mjs enumerates every macOS state I could build (dir 0o111 / 0o000 / 0o444, symlink chains of 8/30/31/32/33/34/40, dangling symlink, resolved path over PATH_MAX through a short symlink, FIFO, /dev/null, firmlink) and in every state where existsSync is true, both realpath forms succeed, so a path the caller has already accepted never makes realpathSync.native throw here. The state was then INJECTED (labelled as a simulation, not a mission): with fs.realpathSync.native replaced by a thrower, the pristine build answers `check --strict --json` exit 0 on mission A with a well-formed JSON payload (the catch returns null and the gate simply has no spelling verdict), while the SAME run with this mutant applied prints `✗ Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'startsWith')` and exits 1 with NO JSON AT ALL. Emptying the catch does not return null: it lets canon stay undefined and crashes one line later, so `--json` stops being JSON — the exact failure the neighbouring unreadable-file handler was written to prevent. On Windows, .native is GetFinalPathNameByHandle, which opens a handle where existsSync only reads attributes, so the catch is reachable on the very platform this function was added for (RWD-2026-0016, the windows-latest leg of 2026-08-17).

Corrected probe and per-mutant-detail on all four missions: identical on every one (mission A exit 1 with the same two violations, B exit 0, C exit 1 with the same two 'resolves to a directory' violations, D exit 0). Mission C was built for this mutant specifically: its two pointers resolve to the base directory, which is the only state where the guard fires at all. Also ran scripts/catch-reachability.mjs, whose table shows plain and native realpath never disagree on this platform in the direction that would let a lexically-contained but really-outside path reach this function (the ELOOP window closes at the same chain length for stat and for the JS walker: at 32 both succeed, at 33 existsSync already fails).
verdicts.argument: The mutant deletes an early `return null`, so it can only change the RESULT in a state where the guard fires — canon not under canonBase + sep — AND where the surviving expression then answers non-null. Both conditions cannot hold together. (1) The function is only called from the branch of resolvePointer that has already established `real === baseAbs || real.startsWith(baseAbs + sep)` on the plain realpath of abs; a pointer whose target escapes the base is resolved by that same call and takes the repository branch instead, where this function is never called. So abs is at the base or strictly below it. (2) canon and canonBase are BOTH realpathSync.native — that is the fix RWD-2026-0016 made, and it is what keeps the prefix true whatever the caller resolved with, since case canonicalisation and 8.3 expansion are applied identically to both sides. Below the base, canon therefore starts with canonBase + sep and the guard never fires: measured on missions A, B and D. (3) The one remaining state is abs === base, canon === canonBase, built in mission C. There `canon.slice(canonBase.length + 1)` is the empty string, and `'' === wrote.toLowerCase() && '' !== wrote` is unsatisfiable for every wrote (empty makes the second conjunct false, non-empty makes the first false), so mutant and original both return null. (4) Independently, that state cannot reach the output anyway: a pointer resolving to a directory is refused by isRegularFile BEFORE the spelling is consulted — mission C prints 'typed pointer resolves to a directory, not a file', with and without the mutant. RESIDUAL, stated rather than hidden: a Windows reparse point, or a plain-realpath failure that made realpathOr hand the caller a lexical path, could in principle break the prefix relation; I could not build either state on macOS, and even there the mutant would need a length coincidence between the unrelated slice and the pointer path to become visible. That residual is the reason this one should be re-read on the windows-latest leg rather than treated as closed forever.

FALSE GREEN, measured. Shipped probe on the self-gate: no observable difference (exit 0, 4416 bytes) — no pointer in runward's own mission has a diverging spelling. split('/') becoming split('') interleaves the separator between every CHARACTER, so src/Guard.TS becomes s/r/c///G/u/a/r/d/./T/S, which normalize() reduces to s/r/c/G/u/a/r/d/T/S; the prefix comparison can then never hold and the rung answers null — 'the spelling is fine' — for every mis-spelled pointer it is consulted on. On m-spelling: pristine exit 1 / 4770 bytes with the case-insensitivity refusal; mutant exit 0 / 4496 bytes, NO violation. A pointer that resolves only because the filesystem is forgiving, and that a Linux CI runner would not find, is accepted and can be sealed. The two controls prove the mutant touches only this rung: m-spelling-control (identical fixture, mission addressed exactly as created, so the segment walk answers instead) is byte-identical under the mutant at exit 1 / 4764 bytes with the same message, and m-base is byte-identical too at exit 0 / 4486 bytes, so there is no false RED either. Nothing in the project catches it: test/unit/evidence-spelling-unmasked.test.js drives the WALK's rungs — its ./ cases exist precisely to defeat this fallback so the walk is on its own — and has no case in which the fallback ANSWERS, so the normalize() added in 0.36.2 and the split('/') feeding it are unguarded everywhere except the windows-latest CI leg, which the unit suite the mutant survived does not run.

verdicts.evidence: Caught in the OTHER direction, by mission B: baseline exit 0 (green) -> exit 1 with 'typed pointer file:code/src/core/domain/guard-alias.ts#guardFields — this filesystem is case-insensitive; on a case-sensitive one (Linux CI) it would not resolve. Forcing the left operand true drops the 'differs only in CASE' test, so any pointer whose resolved path differs from what was typed — every symlink inside a project, including the npm/pnpm workspace pattern the repository branch of resolvePointer was written to support — is refused, with a message naming a cause that is not the cause.
